question: Groups are named after the signature they fit best
decision: Within each cell type, cells with similar expression are grouped, and each group is compared with the published signatures. A group takes the name of the signature it fits best, if the fit is clear (score at least 0.15) and clearly better than the next signature (by at least 0.05). Groups with fewer than 50 cells, with cells from fewer than three samples, or that look like damaged cells stay unnamed.
reason: The score compares each signature with control genes of similar expression (Tirosh et al. 2016), so short and long signatures can be compared fairly. The same thresholds are used for every cell type. Damaged cells are judged against their own study, because single-nucleus data detect fewer genes per cell without being of lower quality.

question: Every signature comes from a published figure or table
decision: Each signature is taken from one figure or table of a published study, cited next to it, and was checked against the full text.
reason: Every name on this page therefore rests on the literature, and the citation next to each signature lets anyone check a name against the original study.

question: Some gene programmes are shown as scores, not names
decision: Programmes that are unreliable as cell names are shown as a score on the map: programmes that tissue handling can switch on, programmes shared with other cell types, and states described only on another platform or in a single small study.
reason: Digesting tissue with collagenase at 37 C switches on the same stress genes in every cell type (O'Flanagan et al. 2019), so cells that differ only in these genes may differ in handling rather than biology.

question: Myeloid lineages follow the established classification
decision: Macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells and neutrophils are labelled as in the original publication of these data; mast cells are a cell type of their own there. Each card shows how many cells agree with a cited set of marker genes.
reason: Myeloid cells have an established naming system based on their developmental origin (Guilliams et al. 2014), and every cell in these data was labelled by it (Loveless et al. 2025).

question: HSP+ and MT+ macrophages are shown as scores
reason: Both states were described in human PDAC (Caronni et al. 2023), but heat-shock genes are also switched on by enzymatic digestion of tissue (O'Flanagan et al. 2019), and metallothionein genes respond to stress in many cell types.

question: The monocyte-like programme of macrophages is shown as a score
reason: IL1B+ inflammatory macrophages come from recruited monocytes and keep classical monocyte genes (Caronni et al. 2023), so a monocyte-like name would cut through that population.

question: Neutrophil states are shown as scores
reason: The four tumour-associated neutrophil states were defined with the BD Rhapsody platform (Wang et al. 2023), whose authors note that most earlier droplet-based (10x) PDAC studies, the technology behind most of these data, detected few neutrophils.

question: C1QC+ and FOLR2+ macrophages overlap
decision: Both signatures are used, but groups that fit them almost equally stay unnamed.
reason: C1QA and C1QC mark all macrophages in human PDAC (Caronni et al. 2023, Extended Data Fig. 1d), and the two signatures share genes (Ma et al. 2022).

question: Almost no plasmacytoid dendritic cells among the myeloid cells
decision: The pDC signature is used, but no myeloid group fitted it.
reason: The pDC gene LILRA4 is found in only about 1% of the cells of every myeloid lineage in these data, so pDCs probably sit outside the myeloid cells. Another study found no pDC cluster among PDAC mononuclear phagocytes either (Caronni et al. 2023).

question: Fibroblast groups are defined based on the literature
decision: The main fibroblast groups, like their sub-groups, are named from published signatures.
reason: Unlike myeloid cells, fibroblasts have no agreed naming system: whether CAF types are fixed lineages or changeable states is still open, and names should follow function (Sahai et al. 2020).

question: iCAFs and myCAFs follow the signatures of Elyada et al. 2019
decision: The human iCAF and myCAF signatures of Elyada et al. 2019 are used unchanged. The iCAF signature names the iCAFs and, together with the resident-like genes, the wider iCAF family.
reason: They are the only fully listed human signatures for the two classical CAF types of PDAC; other studies give a few markers each, which differ in detail.

question: Antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs) are shown as a score
reason: No human PDAC study has resolved a separate apCAF cluster: human apCAF-like cells were mixed with iCAFs (Elyada et al. 2019), CD74 and HLA-DRA occur across human CAFs (Dominguez et al. 2020), and searches in large datasets found none (Oh et al. 2023). In one study the CD74/HLA class II 'apCAF' cluster turned out to be Schwann cells (Chen et al. 2026); in another, apCAF subclusters carried T-, B- and mast-cell genes (Tao et al. 2025), as cell doublets would. HLA-DR from myeloid cells blurs the signal (Cords et al. 2023). In mice, apCAFs arise from mesothelial cells (Huang et al. 2022).

question: The iCAF signature does not follow tissue-handling stress
decision: iCAFs are named with the human iCAF signature of Elyada et al. 2019, unchanged. The stress genes of tissue digestion are shown next to it as a score.
reason: This is the human iCAF signature most PDAC studies refer to. Some iCAF genes (CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL8) are also switched on when tissue is digested with collagenase (O'Flanagan et al. 2019). In these data, among about 16,600 fibroblasts of the iCAF family, the published signature did not rise with the stress genes (correlation 0.05 across cells), whereas a list of cytokines alone did (0.34). Cells fitting the signature came mostly from tumours and metastases and rarely from normal pancreas, as expected for cancer-associated fibroblasts.

question: Mural, mesothelial and Schwann-like cells are set apart
decision: Groups that fit mural-cell, mesothelial or Schwann-cell genes best are shown as separate groups and left out of the fibroblast make-up.
reason: Fibroblasts and mural cells share contractile genes and differ only in combinations of genes (Muhl et al. 2020); Schwann cells have been mistaken for antigen-presenting CAFs in PDAC data (Chen et al. 2026); and mesothelial cells can become CAFs, losing their mesothelial genes on the way (Huang et al. 2022). KRT19 is left out of the mesothelial genes because tumour cells express it too.

question: No group of pancreatic stellate cells
decision: Cells with the 'stellate cell' genes of PDAC single-cell studies fall into the mural-like group. This will be revisited with the pericytes.
reason: There is no specific marker of human stellate cells (Du et al. 2025). The stellate-cell cluster of one PDAC study is defined by RGS5, NOTCH3, NDUFA4L2 and HIGD1B (Chen et al. 2021), which are pericyte genes (Muhl et al. 2020). In normal human pancreas, quiescent stellate cells are marked by FABP4, ADIRF, RGS5, CSPG4 or MCAM (Baron et al. 2016; Tosti et al. 2021), again pericyte genes, and Tosti et al. note that their quiescent stellate cells may include pericytes. Lineage tracing in mice places most pancreatic fibroblasts in one lineage without a separate stellate population (Han et al. 2023).

question: Interferon-response CAFs (ifCAFs) are shown as a score
reason: ifCAFs formed a cluster of their own among FAP+ CAFs sorted from 6 human PDACs, with high myCAF scores (Cumming et al. 2025); the same state appears as ISG+ myCAFs, 1.4% of CAFs (Tao et al. 2025), and as the CXCL10+ fibroblast cluster myFb 5 of Loveless et al. 2025. In these data, only 405 of 58,523 fibroblasts (0.7%) express at least three of the four ifCAF genes of Cumming et al., spread over 11 of the 12 studies, too few to form a group. Interferon genes respond in every cell type, so a score shows where these cells are without forcing a group.

question: LRRC15+ myofibroblasts follow Dominguez et al. 2020
decision: Their 11-gene signature is used, the version they applied to immunotherapy cohorts.
reason: It was derived in 22 human PDACs, where these cells make up about half of all fibroblasts, and later cross-tissue studies recover the same core genes (Krishnamurty et al. 2022; Gao et al. 2024).

question: MMP1+ myofibroblasts are included despite thin PDAC evidence
decision: They are a sub-group; their card says how little evidence there is in PDAC.
reason: Two independent cross-tissue studies find this state, one including pancreas (Steele et al. 2025; Gao et al. 2024); in PDAC only a minor IL11+ population, absent from some studies, has been reported (Oh et al. 2023).

question: CD105 (ENG) does not divide fibroblasts here
reason: The CD105-positive and -negative lineages are defined by protein. In single-cell data the ENG transcript is detected in only part of the cells and is lower in iCAF-like cells, so RNA cannot sort cells into the two (Hutton et al. 2021).

question: No group of Meflin (ISLR)+ cancer-restraining CAFs
reason: ISLR expression is graded and fades as these cells become activated CAFs; the human evidence comes from in situ hybridisation with a 20% cut-off per tumour, not from a distinct cell population (Mizutani et al. 2019).

question: Hypoxic, tumour-like CAFs (tCAFs) are shown as a score
reason: The tCAF genes (MME, NDRG1, ENO1, CA9) are hypoxia and glycolysis genes (Cords et al. 2023), which reflect where a cell sits and are shared with other cell types nearby; tCAF-MME cells were more frequent in PDACs with nerve invasion (Chen et al. 2025).

question: The neural-like CAF programme is shown as a score
reason: It comes from a single preprint with five matched patients and partly overlaps iCAFs (Henstridge et al. 2025). Nerve-associated fibroblasts defined by other genes (NGFR, SCN7A) form a group of their own (Chen et al. 2025).

question: No groups of dividing or vascular CAFs
reason: Dividing CAFs are defined by the cell cycle rather than by a CAF type (Cords et al. 2023; Tao et al. 2025), and cycling cells were removed from these data before summarising. Vascular CAFs could not be told apart from pericytes in PDAC data (Cords et al. 2023), and pericytes are a cell type of their own in these data.

question: CAF types described by a single study are not used
decision: This applies to CDCP1+ FTL+ and TSPAN8+ CAFs (Tao et al. 2025) and to the gene programmes of Hwang et al. 2022, whose gene lists are only in a supplementary table that could not be checked.
reason: A name needs a signature supported by more than one study, or a clear definition in human PDAC with a listed set of genes.

question: Resident-like fibroblasts are a sub-group; csCAFs are a score
decision: Resident-like (C7+) fibroblasts form a sub-group of the iCAF family. The complement genes of complement-secreting CAFs (csCAFs) are shown as a score.
reason: Without this group, many fibroblasts, mostly from normal tissue, fitted no signature. Several independent human studies describe these cells: normal fibroblasts that dominate normal pancreas (Dimitrieva et al. 2024), donor-pancreas fibroblasts that differ from tumour fibroblasts (Carpenter et al. 2023), the COL15A1+ fibroblasts of a cross-tissue study (Gao et al. 2024) and a universal-like cluster of tumour and adjacent tissue (Buechler et al. 2021). Only genes reported by at least two of them are in the signature. csCAFs are about two-thirds of the fibroblasts of normal pancreas and are thought to be resident fibroblasts that persist in tumours (Chen et al. 2026); they share C7, PTGDS, GPX3 and APOE with this signature, so a separate name would split one population.

question: Resident-like fibroblasts and iCAFs form one family
decision: One main group, the iCAF family, is named from the iCAF and resident-like genes together. Resident-like fibroblasts, iCAFs and CCL19+ reticular-like fibroblasts are its sub-groups, separated by a second grouping within the family.
reason: Across all fibroblasts in these data, cells with the iCAF genes (IL6, HAS1, LIF, CCL2) grouped together with cells expressing resident and complement genes (C7, CXCL12, C3). Such groups fitted both signatures almost equally, so with two separate main groups neither could be named; grouping again within the family separates them. iCAFs are thought to arise from resident-like fibroblasts: single-cell data suggest transitions from complement-secreting to inflammatory CAFs (Chen et al. 2026) and from normal fibroblasts to iCAFs (Tao et al. 2025), and both share CFD, PDGFRA and CXCL12 (Tao et al. 2025). The myCAF family is organised the same way.

question: Universal-like and inflammatory fibroblasts overlap
decision: Both groups are used; groups that fit the two almost equally stay unnamed.
reason: The two programmes share genes: an 'inflammatory' fibroblast cluster of chronic pancreatitis and PDAC is marked by CD34, MFAP5 and TNXB, genes of universal fibroblasts (Dimitrieva et al. 2024), and CFD and C7 sit on the universal side of the human stromal axis (Krishnamurty et al. 2022), while CFD is also part of the iCAF signature (Elyada et al. 2019).

question: HOPX+ transitional myofibroblasts form a sub-group of their own
decision: They sit in the myCAF family next to LRRC15+ myofibroblasts.
reason: Two independent studies describe myofibroblasts with HOPX, IGFBP5 and TIMP1 but little LRRC15, placed before LRRC15+ CAFs on inferred trajectories: one in human PDAC and pancreatitis (Dimitrieva et al. 2024), one across tissues including pancreas (Gao et al. 2024). The order of the two states is inferred, not traced.

question: The injury-reactive programme is shown as a score
reason: It comes from one study, where it increased after FOLFIRINOX-based neoadjuvant therapy (Dimitrieva et al. 2024), and it shares genes with the metallothionein programme (Zhou et al. 2022) and with stress responses. As a score it can still be compared between treated and untreated tumours.
